ny_trapps_bouldering.blurb: These boulders are strung out along the Undercliff carriage road beneath the Trapps in the Gunks of New York, running from the bridge toward Skytop. They sit on the same hard quartz conglomerate as the cliffs above. Expect roofs, traverses, cracks and the odd highball, with clusters such as Steel Bridge Boulders, Doug's Roof, the Boxcar area and Pebbles. Problems range from V0 to the V11 range, and a lot of the volume is easy, so there are plenty of warm-ups for a session. A smaller share of roped trad climbing at Sleepy Hollow sits alongside the boulders, and a separate cluster near the Wawarsing lot is reached by a connector trail.

nh_exeter_area_bouldering.blurb: Exeter's boulders are scattered through roughly 500 acres of woods in the New Hampshire seacoast, split by a highway into a larger south side and a smaller north side. Town Forest South holds most of the problems, with Town Forest North and the Exeter Boulder making up much of the rest. The terrain is wooded, with a brook and a lot of wetland, and the boulders are quiet compared with the bigger Northeast venues. The problems are mostly on the easy side, V0 to V3 by a wide margin, with a thinner tail up to about V8, and several cracks and aretes among them. Bugs can be a real nuisance in leaf season.

ar_west_side.blurb: West Side is a long wall of sandstone at Horseshoe Canyon Ranch in north-central Arkansas, near Jasper. It faces east and tends toward shade through the day, so it stays cool. The ten crags run from Crackhouse Alley to the Doomsday Wall, with Walls of Moria, Confederate Cracks and the Arcade among the larger ones, and the style swings from slab to steep. Most of the roped climbing is bolted sport with a good number of trad lines, mostly 5.8 to 5.11, and the cracks include some of the best moderate ones in the state. Bouldering is substantial too, led by Idaho Boulders, with problems from V0 up to V10 and beyond.

me_camden_hills.blurb: The Camden Hills rise on the west shore of Penobscot Bay near Camden, Maine, with views across Megunticook Lake. The cliffs are metamorphic rock, textured and featured, and none of the climbs are very long. Trad is the most common style, mostly 5.7 to 5.11, with a good number of sport routes reaching into the low 5.12s, a boulder area at The Spot, and some ice in winter. Barrett's Cove Cliff, the largest crag, faces southeast and is warm, though its right side stays damp for much of summer. Expect slabby, footwork-heavy trad with protection that can be sparse for the grade, so be solid before leading.

ga_mount_yonah.blurb: Mount Yonah is a granite dome in northeast Georgia, around an hour and a half north of Atlanta, and it works as a local climbing school. Routes are mostly single-pitch with some multi-pitch, mixing trad, sport and top-rope, with grades from about 5.5 to 5.12 and a few harder. Bouldering is a significant part too, mostly at the Parking Lot Boulders, with problems from V0 into the V8 range and beyond. The Main Face has the most routes and faces southwest, so it gets very hot in summer. The Lowers are shadier and more comfortable then. Other walls include Gumby Slab, Super Crack Area and Pin Wall.

wa_banks_lake.blurb: Banks Lake is a lakeside climbing area in central Washington, near Grand Coulee Dam and Steamboat Rock. The rock is granite, and the mix is wide: sport routes lead the count, with plentiful bouldering, a smaller amount of trad and top-rope, and deep-water soloing over the lake. Most roped routes fall between 5.7 and 5.11, and the boulders run from easy to moderate. Roadside Rock and Northrup Canyon are the largest areas. Some crags sit on peninsulas or rise straight out of the water. Spring and fall are the best seasons, summers are hot, wind can blow, and crowds are usually thin. Loose holds happen, and the granite can be hard on skin.
